questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The price you get if you sell now
The price you pay if you buy now
Getting a worse price than you expected
questions.why: You buy at the ask and sell at the lower bid, so the spread is a cost on every round trip.

questions.q: A share is quoted {b}p bid / {a}p ask. You buy {q} shares and sell them straight back. How much do you lose, in £?
questions.why: The spread is ({a}p − {b}p) per share × {q} shares = £{answer}.

questions.q: You put down {m} as margin with {l}:1 leverage. The market moves {d}% against you. How much do you lose, in £?
questions.why: Position = {m} × {l}. {d}% of that is £{answer}, a big share of your margin.

questions.q: You want to buy only if the price is 95p or lower. Which order?
questions.why: A limit order fills only at your price or better.

questions.q: A normal stop-loss always sells at exactly your stop price.
questions.why: It becomes a market order when triggered. If the price gaps past your level, you get the next available price, which can be worse.

questions.q: Why is going short riskier than buying, without a stop?
options: A price can rise without limit, so losses have no ceiling
Shorting is illegal in the UK
questions.why: When you buy, the worst case is the price going to zero. When you short, the price can keep rising.

questions.q: Which of these is a UK rule for retail CFD customers?
options: Leverage capped between 30:1 and 2:1, and you can't lose more than your account
Unlimited leverage if you sign a form
Crypto CFDs are allowed with 50:1 leverage
questions.why: The FCA caps leverage, closes positions at 50% of margin and gives negative balance protection. Crypto derivatives are banned for retail.

questions.q: Match each product to how its profits are usually treated in the UK.
pairs: Treated as gambling: usually no Capital Gains Tax
Taxed as capital gains above the allowance
Shares in a Stocks and Shares ISA
Stamp Duty to buy UK shares, CGT on gains
questions.why: Wrappers and products change the tax. Check HMRC rules for your situation.

questions.q: Shares in a tiny company usually have wider spreads than shares in a FTSE 100 company.
questions.why: Fewer buyers and sellers means less liquidity, so spreads are wider and big orders move the price.

questions.q: Explain why leverage is dangerous for a beginner, even though it can multiply profits.

ideas.label: It multiplies losses as much as gains
A small market move can wipe out much or all of the deposit
It doesn't improve your odds or edge (and costs are magnified too)

questions.model: Leverage multiplies losses exactly as much as gains, so a small move against you (5% at 20:1) can wipe out the whole deposit. It doesn't make you any more likely to be right, and costs are magnified too, so a beginner without an edge just loses faster.

tests.answer: It multiplies losses as well as gains, so a small move can wipe out your deposit, and it doesn't improve your chances.
You can lose your whole deposit.

questions.q: Explain why frequent trading is so expensive even when each trade's costs look tiny.

ideas.label: Costs (spread, commission, overnight fees) are paid on every single trade
Many trades add up to a large share of your money over a year

questions.model: Spreads, commissions and overnight charges are paid on every trade. Each looks tiny, but frequent traders make hundreds of trades a year, so the costs add up to a large share of their money, and any edge must beat that before making a profit.
questions.why: Small costs × many trades = big costs.

tests.answer: You pay the spread and fees on every trade, and over a year lots of trades add up.
